name: gingerbread cake
instructions:
Samin Nosrat's ginger cake from Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat — adapted from the Chez Panisse original. Halved from the source recipe (2 eggs → 1 egg) because it's an overpoweringly sweet, decadent dessert; a full sheet is too much.

MAKES: one 8x8 or 9-inch round pan (~6-8 servings). Serve with AMERICAN BUTTERCREAM FROSTING (my strong preference — the butteriness balances the high spice load; see FROSTING note). Samin suggests vanilla whipped cream or cream cheese frosting; both work but buttercream is the top pick.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

Ginger-sugar paste:
- 1/2 cup (2 oz) peeled, thinly sliced fresh ginger (~2 1/2 oz unpeeled)
- 1/2 cup (3.5 oz / 100g) sugar

Wet:
- 1/2 cup neutral oil (vegetable, avocado)
- 1/2 cup molasses
- 1/2 cup boiling water
- 1 large egg (added LAST after the batter cools — see procedure)

Dry (all amounts halved from Samin's 2-egg original — for 1 egg):
- scant 1 1/4 cups (6 oz / 170g) all-purpose flour  [from 2 1/3 cups]
- 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon  [from 1 tsp]
- 1/2 tsp ground ginger  [from 1 tsp]
- 1/4 tsp ground cloves  [from 1/2 tsp — LESS if you're worried about clove-forward, see SPICES note]
- 1/8 tsp freshly ground black pepper  [from 1/4 tsp]
- 1 tsp kosher salt or 1/2 tsp fine sea salt  [from 2 tsp / 1 tsp]
- 1 tsp baking soda  [from 2 tsp]

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. PREHEAT the oven to 350°F. Set a rack in the upper third of the oven. Grease an 8x8 or 9-inch round cake pan and line with parchment.
2. GINGER-SUGAR PASTE: put the peeled sliced ginger and sugar in a food processor. Process until it becomes a sugary paste — the ginger breaks down and coats itself in the sugar. Scrape down as needed.
3. DRY BOWL: whisk together the flour, cinnamon, ground ginger, cloves, black pepper, salt, and baking soda in a large bowl.
4. WET BOWL: transfer the ginger-sugar paste to a separate bowl. Add the oil and molasses; stir to combine. Pour in the boiling water and stir — this is what activates the baking soda and brings the batter together.
5. FOLD WET INTO DRY: pour the hot ginger-molasses mixture into the dry ingredients. Fold with a spatula until combined.
6. LET COOL, THEN ADD EGG LAST: wait until the batter has cooled to warm-not-hot (a few minutes) — if you add the egg while the batter is still hot from the boiling water, IT WILL SCRAMBLE. Crack in the egg and whisk it through. The batter will be VERY RUNNY at this point — that's correct.
7. POUR into the prepared pan and bake ~35-45 min (halved batch, shallower pan → less time than the original 9-inch pair). Done when a skewer inserted in the center comes out clean and the top springs back to a light press.
8. COOL in the pan for 15 min before unmolding. Serve warm or room temp with american buttercream frosting (top pick — see FROSTING note), or whipped cream / cream cheese frosting as valid alternatives.
notes:
Samin Nosrat's adaptation of the Chez Panisse ginger cake, from Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat. HALVED here from the source: original is 2 eggs and makes two 9-inch layers; this is 1 egg and one pan.

=== WHY HALVED — TOO DECADENT AT FULL SIZE ===

This is an overpoweringly sweet, molasses-and-oil-heavy dessert. A full sheet or a two-layer cake is more of it than any sitting can absorb. Halving to 1 egg gives you a single 8x8 or 9-inch round that reads as an actual portion rather than a project.

=== FRESH GINGER ROOT IS NOT OVERPOWERING (SURPRISING) ===

Half a cup of fresh ginger sounds like a lot — it isn't. The food-processor step breaks it down into a paste that distributes evenly through the batter, and the long bake mellows it further. It reads as warmth and depth, not sharp ginger-shot heat. Don't be tempted to cut it back.

=== POWDERED SPICES CAN BE OVERPOWERING — ESPECIALLY CLOVES ===

The opposite is true for the ground spices, particularly cloves. Cloves are aggressive and can dominate the cake's whole aromatic profile if you're heavy-handed. The 1/4 tsp here (halved from Samin's 1/2 tsp) is already at the edge — if you want a more balanced ginger-forward cake, cut it to 1/8 tsp or omit. Cinnamon and ground ginger are less aggressive but still real; measure carefully.

Counterintuitive vs the fresh ginger note: the WHOLE fresh root reads gentle, the DRIED powder reads loud. Bakers tend to swap them one-for-one and get burned.

=== GINGER-SUGAR PASTE FIRST — THIS IS THE UNUSUAL STEP ===

Most cake recipes start with creaming or dry-plus-wet. This one starts by processing the sliced fresh ginger with the sugar until it's a paste. The sugar acts as an abrasive that helps the food processor break down the fibrous ginger, and the paste distributes the fresh ginger through the batter uniformly (you don't want fibrous strands or hot pockets of ginger).

=== ADD THE EGG LAST — AFTER THE BATTER COOLS ===

The boiling water goes in early to activate the baking soda + molasses. If you crack the egg into a still-hot batter, IT WILL SCRAMBLE — you'll end up with cooked bits of egg suspended in your batter. Let the batter cool to warm-not-hot (a few minutes' patience) before adding the egg.

=== VERY RUNNY BATTER — THAT'S CORRECT ===

This batter pours like a thick liquid rather than dolloping like a cake batter. That's not a mistake — the high oil, molasses, and boiling-water content make it thin, and the flour hydrates further as it bakes. Just pour it into the pan.

=== NEUTRAL OIL, NOT OLIVE ===

Olive oil clashes with the molasses + spice register (goes bitter-vegetal against the caramel-warmth base). Use vegetable, avocado, or another neutral oil. If all you have is olive, this is a fine cake to wait on.

=== FROSTING — AMERICAN BUTTERCREAM IS THE TOP PICK ===

My strong preference: AMERICAN BUTTERCREAM FROSTING on this cake. The BUTTERINESS balances the high spice load (cinnamon + ground ginger + cloves + black pepper is a lot of aromatic pressure) — the fat in the buttercream mellows the spice register into something rich and cohesive rather than punishing. American buttercream specifically (butter + powdered sugar + vanilla + a splash of milk/cream) works better here than lighter/less-buttery options.

SAMIN'S ALTERNATIVES — WHIPPED CREAM OR CREAM CHEESE FROSTING (BOTH VALID, BOTH SECOND-CHOICE):

- WHIPPED CREAM (Samin's original — 'Vanilla Cream' = whipped cream + vanilla). The unsweetened dairy cuts through the molasses richness. Works — but doesn't add the buttery weight that this specific cake benefits from. Best when you want something lighter alongside.
- CREAM CHEESE FROSTING (Samin also suggests). Also works, but cream cheese frosting is more at home on CARROT CAKE or [[sweet-potato-cornbread]] — cakes where the tang of the cream cheese complements a sweeter, more vegetable-forward cake base. On this heavily-spiced molasses cake, the cream cheese tang competes with the spice rather than balancing it; the butter-forward register of buttercream complements better.

VANILLA ICE CREAM also works if you want a serve-with rather than a proper frosting.

SKIPPING THE DAIRY ACCOMPANIMENT entirely makes the cake read heavier than it needs to. Something buttery / creamy / cool alongside is important; the specific choice of buttercream vs whipped cream vs ice cream is secondary to just having one of them.

=== PAN & BAKE TIME ADJUSTMENTS FOR THE HALVED VERSION ===

One 8x8 square or 9-inch round. Bake ~35-45 min (down from the original's larger two-pan bake). Watch the center — this is a wet batter and it can look done on the surface while the middle is still liquid. Skewer-in-center clean is the real signal.
original_chef: Samin Nosrat (Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat) — adapted from the Chez Panisse gingerbread cake
